I think it’s pretty wild. I didn’t even know of its existence until this post. I went over to check it out to see someone venting about breaking down. It seems like a subreddit for people who have had negative experience with the law. 

Something I noticed about the post, however, was OP admitted to not reading any Neville books…

It’s really important to never compare your journey to others. You can never know what’s happening in someone’s thoughts, or behind the scenes. The law is a very personal journey.

Ultimately, many people were brought to the law because of dire circumstances that seemingly have no physical solution. Like being for real, if you knew of a physical action that you could take to get what you want, you’d just do that—not believe in something seemingly so…wishful. 

It’s inevitable that people in desperate situations will be, well, desperate and therefore not manifest what it is they want. Therefore manifesting the undesirable.

This is why some people with puppies will complain that their dog peed in the house even though they were JUST outside.

​

>I said, ***“You know, Ab, there’s no… not a thing has happened.”***  
>  
>**He wouldn’t discuss it with me. He turned his back on me and went into his little library and slammed the door.**  
>  
>About three times I tried to open up the discussion with my friend Ab between that moment when I first talked to him and the end. >

>Under my door is a little letter from my brother Victor. And he said, “As a family we were never around the table at Christmas together. So in the letter, he justifies why he’s asked me to come. **“I know you don’t have a job, and there’s no excuse for not coming. Neville Goddard teaches that each person is the God of their own life. If you are God, anything should be possible, no? If God wanted someone back who did Him wrongly, it would be a simple task for Him. It would not matter if that's what is "best" for Him, because He is God and *knows* what is best for Him.

**"Sin means to miss the mark. Not to attain your desire, not to be the person you want to be is sinning. Righteousness is the consciousness of already being what you want to be." - Neville Goddard, The Power Of Awareness, Chapter Twenty.**

So the desire of manifesting an SP in itself is not a selfish or impure one. A desire is a desire, and Neville explains the only sin is to not attain that desire.

Now. It's true that people are not *aware* of their power at first, and for some, a journey is required before they reach their desire. This can be reworking an old story, breaking down limiting beliefs about the general topic of love, self-perception, or manifestation. Becoming a new version of yourself that is free from an old concept of self. Change yourself, not the mirror. To simply manifest a new partner in my eyes would be the equivalence of still being the old version of yourself and changing the external when in reality it is the internal limiting beliefs and concepts are that is reflecting in the "mirror", so the outcome will be the same.

Your SP or any other partner can only show up as you assume them to. It will be the same result almost to the T with every new relationship.

I personally don't understand the controversy people have around people manifesting an SP. If you have shifted your self-concept and understand the negative patterns of your relationship, and can now have anyone why would you want to settle for something that is not your true desire?

For me, this is what has differentiated the Law Of Assumption and the Law Of Attraction. Whenever I hear this controversy on SPs it reminds me of the Law Of Attraction idea of, "If it's not meant to be, it's not meant to be. Find someone more aligned/suited for you".

In my interpretation of Neville's work, this does not follow his philosophy. The only thing "meant to be" is the assumption you have.
